I've seen this graph on social networks and the such and I must point out that, while factual, the stats presented are indeed shown in a misleading way.

Most people (and experts, but I'm too lazy to search for a source right now) agree that is not the same to die at, say, age 25, than at age 85, therefore mortality graphs (for judging and policymaking) take into account years of loss. This works by setting an expected age of death (If I recall correctly, chosen as mean age of death plus one standard deviation) and computing how many years of expected life are lost to a cause of death (considering negative values as 0).

This results in cancer and cardiovascular conditions becoming much less prevalent and car accidents and drug overdoses jumping up quite a few places, changing the graph drastically.

In the end, recognizing that human beigns are not immortal, it's up to each one of us to choose what's more important, but I think it's worth indicating that this graph is not telling the full story.
